Deemed
DEEMD
v. (past tense; judged, supposed, concluded)
From Old English deman, to judge, from dom, judgment, the root also behind doom and deemster. The Greek huponoeo means to suspect or surmise, from hupo (under) and noeo (to perceive).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the fourteenth night of the storm off Malta the sailors form a judgment from the sound of the sea: “But when the fourteenth night was come, as we were driven up and down in Adria, about midnight the shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country” (Acts 27:27). To deem is to judge or surmise; the Greek means to suspect, and what follows is the sounding of the lead, twenty fathoms and then fifteen. This is seamanship of a high order, and Luke records it with a sailor's precision. But the ship's safety had already been settled, and not by soundings: “Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Acts 27:25). Paul had the promise; the shipmen had the lead line; and the outcome vindicated both, for God's word was fulfilled through the ordinary labour of men who worked the ship: “And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land” (Acts 27:44). Divine certainty does not retire human diligence; it employs it.

Act 27:27 — "But when the fourteenth night was come, as we were driven up and down in Adria, about midnight the shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country;"

Act 27:25 — "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me."

Act 27:44 — "And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land."

Modern Corruption

God's decree is set against human action, so that either the promise is used to excuse negligence or diligence is trusted as though no promise had been given.

expand to see more

Acts 27 is the clearest narrative in Scripture on the relation of decree to means, and it is routinely read as if it taught only one of them. The fatalist reading says Paul had the promise, so the soundings and the boats and the cutting of the anchors were irrelevant theatre. The practical atheist reading says the crew saved the ship, and the promise was a pious frame around good seamanship.

Luke writes both into one chapter deliberately. God had promised that not a life would be lost; and Paul tells the centurion that if the sailors escape in the boat the rest cannot be saved, insists that the men eat, and lets the soldiers cut the ropes. The promise was certain and it was fulfilled through fourteen nights of hard work and a timely deeming of the shipmen. Scripture's doctrine of providence establishes means rather than abolishing them, which is why prayer and labour belong in the same hand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English deman, to judge, from dom; Greek huponoeo, to surmise; Acts 27:27 has the shipmen deeming land near.
